data_source_comments:
Hello, 
On Wednesday 9/27 I (and many others on the beach) saw a whale swimming along New Brighton Beach on Monterey Bay in Santa Cruz county. I’m curious about ID on the whale because it looked completely unlike a humpback, also smaller but not a sea lion or other mammal - definitely a whale. It was surfacing to breathe and not doing a high arch like a humpback but more of just putting its nose up then back under for 45 seconds to a minute or longer. The nose/face was very crusted in barnacles to the point of being brownish. I didn’t see dorsal or pectoral fins. It was heading north along the beach and then turned north west and went out of view in the distance. In trying to find what type of whale this may have been, the only photos I can find of other whales that look similar are gray whales, but it seems as though this isn’t the correct time of year for them. I’m wondering  if someone at your organization could offer any insight as I’m super curious about what type of whale i saw. Thank you!

data_source_comments:
Gray Whale (assuming based on migration time and the fact that there is a calf) and calf seemly resting as they stayed in one area for roughly an hour. There were at least 3 fluke breaches Roughly 1/3 of a mile out from shore. Another plume of mist signified another whale, slightly south of the calf and mother an hour into their resting. The calf and mother then moved north seemly and other plumes were seen to the south. I am thinking there are more than 3, but I wanted to be conservative because I know for sure there are three. 

The photo I included is of one of the plumes of the mother and calf where they were resting close to shore.

profile.name: spotter
data_source_comments: Was going for a boat ride with my dad on Tuesday afternoon/evening out of narrow river, Narragansett. We first saw something that looked like a whale south of us on the horizon, but couldn’t tell for sure. As they moved north toward us we saw at least one breach, and eventually saw multiple surfacing at the same time, one of which seemed very large. We could only confirm 3 but there may have been 4 or 5 of them. They were last seen about halfway between whale rock and beavertail point. We’re fairly confident they were humpbacks because of the dorsal fin and the knobby heads. Unfortunately, neither of us had our phones and we’re not able to take any photos

profile.name: spotter
data_source_comments: Was going for a boat ride with my dad on Tuesday afternoon/evening out of narrow river, Narragansett. We first saw something that looked like a whale south of us on the horizon, but couldn’t tell for sure. As they moved north toward us we saw at least one breach, and eventually saw multiple surfacing at the same time, one of which seemed very large. We could only confirm 3 but there may have been 4 or 5 of them. They were last seen about halfway between whale rock and beavertail point. We’re fairly confident they were humpbacks because of the dorsal fin and the knobby heads. Unfortunately, neither of us had our phones and we’re not able to take any photos

profile.name: spotter
data_source_comments: Was going for a boat ride with my dad on Tuesday afternoon/evening out of narrow river, Narragansett. We first saw something that looked like a whale south of us on the horizon, but couldn’t tell for sure. As they moved north toward us we saw at least one breach, and eventually saw multiple surfacing at the same time, one of which seemed very large. We could only confirm 3 but there may have been 4 or 5 of them. They were last seen about halfway between whale rock and beavertail point. We’re fairly confident they were humpbacks because of the dorsal fin and the knobby heads. Unfortunately, neither of us had our phones and we’re not able to take any photos

data_source_comments: Was going for a boat ride with my dad on Tuesday afternoon/evening out of narrow river, Narragansett. We first saw something that looked like a whale south of us on the horizon, but couldn’t tell for sure. As they moved north toward us we saw at least one breach, and eventually saw multiple surfacing at the same time, one of which seemed very large. We could only confirm 3 but there may have been 4 or 5 of them. They were last seen about halfway between whale rock and beavertail point. We’re fairly confident they were humpbacks because of the dorsal fin and the knobby heads. Unfortunately, neither of us had our phones and we’re not able to take any photos

profile.name: spotter
data_source_comments: Was going for a boat ride with my dad on Tuesday afternoon/evening out of narrow river, Narragansett. We first saw something that looked like a whale south of us on the horizon, but couldn’t tell for sure. As they moved north toward us we saw at least one breach, and eventually saw multiple surfacing at the same time, one of which seemed very large. We could only confirm 3 but there may have been 4 or 5 of them. They were last seen about halfway between whale rock and beavertail point. We’re fairly confident they were humpbacks because of the dorsal fin and the knobby heads. Unfortunately, neither of us had our phones and we’re not able to take any photos

data_source_comments: Was going for a boat ride with my dad on Tuesday afternoon/evening out of narrow river, Narragansett. We first saw something that looked like a whale south of us on the horizon, but couldn’t tell for sure. As they moved north toward us we saw at least one breach, and eventually saw multiple surfacing at the same time, one of which seemed very large. We could only confirm 3 but there may have been 4 or 5 of them. They were last seen about halfway between whale rock and beavertail point. We’re fairly confident they were humpbacks because of the dorsal fin and the knobby heads. Unfortunately, neither of us had our phones and we’re not able to take any photos

profile.name: spotter
data_source_comments: Was going for a boat ride with my dad on Tuesday afternoon/evening out of narrow river, Narragansett. We first saw something that looked like a whale south of us on the horizon, but couldn’t tell for sure. As they moved north toward us we saw at least one breach, and eventually saw multiple surfacing at the same time, one of which seemed very large. We could only confirm 3 but there may have been 4 or 5 of them. They were last seen about halfway between whale rock and beavertail point. We’re fairly confident they were humpbacks because of the dorsal fin and the knobby heads. Unfortunately, neither of us had our phones and we’re not able to take any photos

profile.name: spotter
data_source_comments: Was going for a boat ride with my dad on Tuesday afternoon/evening out of narrow river, Narragansett. We first saw something that looked like a whale south of us on the horizon, but couldn’t tell for sure. As they moved north toward us we saw at least one breach, and eventually saw multiple surfacing at the same time, one of which seemed very large. We could only confirm 3 but there may have been 4 or 5 of them. They were last seen about halfway between whale rock and beavertail point. We’re fairly confident they were humpbacks because of the dorsal fin and the knobby heads. Unfortunately, neither of us had our phones and we’re not able to take any photos

profile.name: spotter
data_source_comments: Was going for a boat ride with my dad on Tuesday afternoon/evening out of narrow river, Narragansett. We first saw something that looked like a whale south of us on the horizon, but couldn’t tell for sure. As they moved north toward us we saw at least one breach, and eventually saw multiple surfacing at the same time, one of which seemed very large. We could only confirm 3 but there may have been 4 or 5 of them. They were last seen about halfway between whale rock and beavertail point. We’re fairly confident they were humpbacks because of the dorsal fin and the knobby heads. Unfortunately, neither of us had our phones and we’re not able to take any photos

profile.name: spotter
data_source_comments: Was going for a boat ride with my dad on Tuesday afternoon/evening out of narrow river, Narragansett. We first saw something that looked like a whale south of us on the horizon, but couldn’t tell for sure. As they moved north toward us we saw at least one breach, and eventually saw multiple surfacing at the same time, one of which seemed very large. We could only confirm 3 but there may have been 4 or 5 of them. They were last seen about halfway between whale rock and beavertail point. We’re fairly confident they were humpbacks because of the dorsal fin and the knobby heads. Unfortunately, neither of us had our phones and we’re not able to take any photos

Both whales appeared to be adult humpbacks.

Whale then turned approximately 90° and swam out towards the horizon. At approximately 14:45 hrs a second whale was spotted about 100 yards offshore heading east to west. There were many recreational fishing boats nearby, at least a half dozen dolphins patrolling the waters, and multiple gannets diving for fish in the vicinity. Very active waters today. Both whales appeared to be adult humpbacks.

profile.name: spotter
data_source_comments:
Saw humpback with pod of dolphins off the Santa Barbara Cemetery while outrigger canoeing with 5 other people in the canoe.  We all saw the large spout of the whale first.  Then as the animals all came closer we saw it on the surface and dive shallowly numerous times.  We could see the bumps on the head, the dorsal fin, and once it turned and poked its white flipper out of the water.  Quite an amazing sight to see less than .5 mile from shore.  In all our many years of kayaking and canoeing no one of us had ever seen a humpback just offshore in Santa Barbara.  Hawaii, yes, but never here.  
 
For some reason the location is showing my house, but I can’t show the location where we saw the humpback.

photo_url: About an hour later, J and K pods were spread out from Hannah Heights to Eagle Point. A few individual whales were foraging offshore while a few small groups were spread out closer to shore. The new J pod calf was found inshore in a small group just north of Eagle Point. The calf was traveling with J31 but several other young females were with them too as the whales turned back north again. J40 and J46 seemed particularly interested in the new calf. L87 also traveled briefly behind this group. Other small groups were in the area including one that had K16, K35, and J45 socializing together. K38 and J51 were still playing with each other.

data_source_comments: visual entry: Yesterday (July 31), J-Pod was joined by a large portion of L-Pod in the Salish Sea. We saw them as they headed north past Lime Kiln in the late afternoon. J47 Notch, pictured here, has, when we have seen him, been going back and forth between his grieving mother J35 Tahlequah and hanging out with some other young males in J-Pod. Yesterday he was in with J38 Cookie and L105 Fluke, among others. J50 Scarlet was present also. (The August 1 update is J35 Tahlequah is still carrying her deceased daughter, for nine days now. It's difficult to imagine what she has been going through or the effort required to carry her baby hundreds of miles. We hope she finds the right time to let go, and that the body of her newborn returns peacefully to the sea. We are all struggling alongside her as we watch from afar, with a renewed fire to do whatever we can on behalf of the Southern Residents.) -Monika Wieland Shields, OBI
